lead: Nearest-neighbour methods assume the answer changes slowly near the query. Local methods keep that assumption but do more than vote. Locally weighted regression fits a fresh small model around each query. A radial basis function network adds up fixed Gaussian bumps at chosen centres. Case-based reasoning stores whole solved problems and adapts the closest one. You meet them in house-price estimates, soft sensors in process plants, and help-desk systems that suggest the fix used on a similar ticket.
prereq: You need: 3.6 kNN for the neighbour idea, and weighted least squares from Unit 2, Regression and Model Evaluation.

blocks.text: kNN predicts by averaging the labels of nearby training points. When the target rises or falls steadily with x, a straight line through those neighbours beats a flat average. Locally weighted regression (LWR) does that: for each query x it fits a fresh weighted model, giving nearby training points more say than distant ones.

blocks.where: x_i is a training input, x is the query, τ is the bandwidth (same units as x, τ > 0), and w_i is the weight of training point i. w_i lies between 0 and 1, and w_i = 1 when x_i = x.

blocks.text: τ sets the width of the neighbourhood. A small τ lets only very close points count, so the fitted curve can wiggle and follow noise. A large τ makes all weights close to 1, and LWR turns into ordinary least squares over the whole data set.

items: Store every training pair (x_i, y_i) and fit nothing in advance — LWR is a lazy learner.
For a query x, compute w_i for every training point.
Minimise Σ w_i (y_i − a − b·x_i)² to get a local straight line.
Predict a + b·x at the query.

blocks.text: a = (S_y·S_xx − S_x·S_xy) / (S·S_xx − S_x²),  b = (S·S_xy − S_x·S_y) / (S·S_xx − S_x²)
blocks.where: S = Σ w_i, S_x = Σ w_i x_i, S_xx = Σ w_i x_i², S_y = Σ w_i y_i, S_xy = Σ w_i x_i y_i; a is the local intercept and b the local slope.

blocks.text: Each query rebuilds the sums and solves a small linear system, roughly O(n·d²) work for n points and d features, so LWR is slow when queries arrive fast. The training data must also stay available at prediction time.
An RBF network places a few Gaussian bumps in input space and learns how much each contributes to the output. Hidden units compute bumps; the output unit is linear.
φ_j(x) = exp(−||x − μ_j||² / (2σ_j²)),   y(x) = b + Σ_j w_j φ_j(x)
blocks.where: μ_j is the centre vector of hidden unit j, σ_j is its width, ||·|| is Euclidean distance, φ_j(x) is that unit's activation (between 0 and 1), w_j is its output weight, and b is a bias.

blocks.text: Each hidden unit answers one question: how close is the query to my centre? Because the output is linear in w_j, the weights come from ordinary least squares once centres and widths are fixed.

items: Choose centres: random training points, a grid, or k-means on the inputs (Unit 4, K-means clustering).
Set each width, for example to the average distance to the nearest centres.
Solve least squares for w_j and b, using the activations as features.

blocks.text: LWR puts one bump on every training point and refits at every query. An RBF network keeps a handful of fixed bumps and one weight vector shared by all queries, so prediction is a short sum. That speed is why RBF networks appear in soft sensors, control loops and small classifiers. Only some syllabi teach them here; others leave them for Unit 5.

Case-based reasoning (CBR) solves a new problem by remembering old ones. A case stores the problem, the solution that was used, and the outcome. Nothing is compressed into a model; the cases themselves are the knowledge.

items: Retrieve: score stored cases with a similarity measure and take the k closest (see 3.6 kNN).
Reuse: copy the best case's solution, or adapt it to the differences.
Revise: test the proposed solution, in simulation or with a human, and repair it if it fails.
Retain: store the new problem and its verified solution as a case.

blocks.text: The similarity measure decides quality. For numeric features use a weighted Euclidean distance; for symbolic features count matching attributes or use distance in a taxonomy. Weights come from domain experts, so scaling matters: a salary in rupees must not swamp an age in years.

Example: a bank's loan desk keeps past applications with their repayment outcomes. A new application is matched to similar past ones and a decision is proposed, then reviewed. CBR is easy to explain because you can show the retrieved case, and it learns from a single new example. Its costs are case-base upkeep — duplicates, outdated cases — and weak generalisation when nothing similar is stored.
The three differ in what they store and what they do at query time.

examples.question: Training points are (x=0, y=1), (x=1, y=2) and (x=2, y=4). Use locally weighted regression with a Gaussian weight and bandwidth τ = 1 to predict y at the query x = 1. Use a local straight line y = a + b·x. Find the three weights, the weighted sums, a, b and the prediction.
examples.answer: The local linear fit is y = 0.774 + 1.500x, giving a prediction of 2.274 at x = 1.
examples.check:
import math
pts=[(0.0,1.0),(1.0,2.0),(2.0,4.0)]
q=1.0
tau=1.0
w=[math.exp(-((x-q)**2)/(2*tau*tau)) for x,y in pts]
S=sum(w)
Sx=sum(wi*x for wi,(x,y) in zip(w,pts))
Sxx=sum(wi*x*x for wi,(x,y) in zip(w,pts))
Sy=sum(wi*y for wi,(x,y) in zip(w,pts))
Sxy=sum(wi*x*y for wi,(x,y) in zip(w,pts))
det=S*Sxx-Sx*Sx
a=(Sy*Sxx-Sx*Sxy)/det
b=(S*Sxy-Sx*Sy)/det
pred=a+b*q
for v in [w[0],w[1],w[2],S,Sx,Sxx,Sy,Sxy,a,b,pred]:
    print(round(v,3))

traps: LWR is lazy: no model exists until a query arrives, and the weights and fit are recomputed for every query. Never describe it as trained once in advance.

An RBF network is not the SVM RBF kernel of 3.7. The SVM uses the Gaussian form as a similarity between points inside a margin maximiser; the RBF network has explicit centres and learned output weights.
LWR, τ too large: every weight is nearly 1, so the local fit collapses to one global straight line and misses curvature. τ too small: the curve follows noise.

RBF network, σ too large: every bump flattens, activations approach 1, the output barely changes with x, and the network loses all locality — a nearly constant, over-smooth function. σ too small: bumps are very narrow, activations fall to near 0 between centres, the design matrix turns ill-conditioned, and predictions go spiky away from the centres.
Gaussian weights are similarities, not probabilities. They do not sum to 1, and all of them can be tiny when the query is far from every training point.

CBR fails quietly when the similarity measure is wrong: unscaled features or renamed attributes make retrieval return cases that look close but are not. Fix scaling and weights before blaming the case base.

quiz.q: Write the Gaussian weight used in locally weighted regression and say what τ controls.
quiz.a: w_i = exp(−(x_i − x)²/(2τ²)). τ is the bandwidth: it sets the width of the neighbourhood in units of x.

quiz.q: Why is locally weighted regression called a lazy learner?
quiz.a: It stores the training data and fits nothing until a query arrives. For each query it recomputes all weights and solves the weighted least-squares problem again.

quiz.q: An RBF network has one hidden unit with centre μ = 2 and width σ = 1, output weight w = 3 and bias b = 0. Find the output at x = 3.
In the worked example, if τ is made very large, what prediction do you get at x = 1?
quiz.a: All weights approach 1, so the fit tends to ordinary least squares over the three points: a = 0.833, b = 1.500, prediction 0.833 + 1.500 = 2.333 at x = 1.

quiz.q: LWR and an RBF network both use Gaussians. Give two differences that decide which one you deploy.
quiz.a: LWR places one Gaussian on every training point and refits weights per query, so training is free but prediction is slow and needs the data. An RBF network uses a few chosen centres and one weight vector learned once, so training costs more but prediction is a short dot product. LWR also degrades in high dimensions where distances lose meaning.

quiz.q: A CBR help desk stops finding good matches after a product upgrade renames its modules. Give the likely cause and one fix.
quiz.a: The attribute names and values changed, so the similarity measure no longer aligns new problems with old cases. Re-map the old case features, re-weight the similarity measure, and retire cases that describe the old product.

quiz.q: List the four steps of the case-based reasoning cycle.

beyond: Not for the exam. Gaussian process regression is the Bayesian version of LWR: instead of one weighted fit per query it returns a mean and a variance, so the model states how unsure it is. RBF networks were a stepping stone to kernel methods. CBR survives in recommender systems and in maintenance logs that suggest the fix used for a similar machine.
